questions.question: Two paper strips are exactly the same length. Strip A is cut into 4 equal parts and 3 of those parts are coloured. Strip B is cut into 8 equal parts and 5 of those parts are coloured. Which strip has the greater coloured amount?
options: Strip A (3/4), because 3/4 = 6/8 and 6/8 is greater than 5/8
Strip B (5/8), because 5 coloured parts is more than 3 coloured parts
Strip B (5/8), because eighths are bigger pieces than fourths
They are the same, because both strips are the same length
questions.explain: Make the denominators match first: 3/4 = 6/8, and 6/8 > 5/8, so Strip A is greater. The usual trap is counting coloured parts (5 beats 3) — numerators only decide the winner when the parts are the same size.

questions.question: Mia and Jon each have a grid of the same size. Mia colours 5 of her 6 equal squares. Jon colours 8 of his 12 equal squares. Which statement is true?
options: 8/12 is greater, because 8 is greater than 5
5/6 is greater, because 5/6 = 10/12 and 10/12 is greater than 8/12
8/12 is greater, because twelfths are larger pieces than sixths
5/6 and 8/12 are equal, because both grids are the same size
questions.explain: Rename 5/6 in twelfths by multiplying top and bottom by 2: 5/6 = 10/12, which is more than 8/12. The trap is thinking more coloured squares means more of the grid — Jon's squares are smaller, so his 8 do not go as far.

questions.question: Two identical water jugs are marked in equal parts. One jug is filled to 2 of its 3 equal parts. The other is filled to 7 of its 12 equal parts. Which jug has less water?
options: The 2/3 jug, because 2 is less than 7
The 2/3 jug, because 12 is a bigger denominator than 3, so 7/12 has to be the bigger fraction
The 7/12 jug, because 2/3 = 8/12 and 7/12 is less than 8/12
Neither — thirds and twelfths cannot be compared at all
questions.explain: Rewrite 2/3 in twelfths (multiply top and bottom by 4) to get 8/12, so 7/12 is the smaller amount. Watch out for the idea that a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction — 12 equal parts are smaller parts, not larger ones.

questions.question: One chocolate bar is broken into 5 equal pieces and 4 pieces are eaten. An identical bar is broken into 10 equal pieces and 7 pieces are eaten. From which bar was more chocolate eaten?
options: From the bar in 10 pieces, because 7 pieces eaten is more than 4 pieces eaten
From the bar in 10 pieces, because tenths are bigger than fifths
The same amount, because each bar still has some pieces left
From the bar in 5 pieces, because 4/5 = 8/10 and 8/10 is greater than 7/10
questions.explain: Give both fractions the same denominator: 4/5 = 8/10, and 8/10 > 7/10, so more was eaten from the bar cut into 5 pieces. Counting pieces is the trap — 7 small tenths are still less than 4 big fifths.

questions.question: Which sign makes this true, and why?  5/8 ___ 2/3
options: <, because 5/8 = 15/24 and 2/3 = 16/24, so 15/24 is less than 16/24
>, because 5 is greater than 2
>, because 8 is a bigger denominator than 3
=, because 5/8 and 2/3 are both close to the benchmark 1/2
questions.explain: Use 24 as a common denominator: 5/8 = 15/24 and 2/3 = 16/24, so 5/8 < 2/3. Being near the same benchmark does not make two fractions equal — you still have to rename them with a shared denominator.

questions.question: Which comparison is TRUE?
questions.explain: Rename to a common denominator: 3/4 = 6/8, which is greater than 5/8. The other statements come from comparing only the top numbers or only the bottom numbers — for example 1/6 is smaller than 1/4 because splitting a whole into 6 parts makes each part smaller.

questions.question: Leo and Ana have identical 1 L water bottles. Leo's bottle is 3/4 full and Ana's bottle is 7/12 full. Who has more water?
options: Ana, because 7 is more than 3
Ana, because twelfths are bigger parts than quarters
Leo, because 3/4 = 9/12 and 9/12 is greater than 7/12
They have the same amount, because 3/4 and 7/12 are both more than 1/2
questions.explain: Twelve is a multiple of four, so rename 3/4 as 9/12 and compare: 9/12 > 7/12, so Leo has more. Two fractions can both sit above the 1/2 benchmark and still be different — the benchmark narrows it down but does not finish the job.

questions.question: Sam wrote the fractions 3/8, 5/6 and 2/3 on the board. Which list puts them in order from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Rename all three in twenty-fourths: 3/8 = 9/24, 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/6 = 20/24, so the order is 3/8, then 2/3, then 5/6. Ordering by the top numbers (2, 3, 5) or by the bottom numbers (3, 6, 8) gives the wrong list because the pieces are different sizes.

questions.question: Jayden says: ‘3/8 is greater than 2/3, because 3 is greater than 2.’ Is he correct?
options: No. In twenty-fourths, 3/8 = 9/24 and 2/3 = 16/24, so 3/8 is actually less than 2/3
Yes, because to compare fractions you compare the numerators
Yes, and eighths are bigger pieces than thirds because 8 is greater than 3
No — you cannot tell without seeing a picture, because the denominators are different
questions.explain: Numerators can only be compared once the denominators match, so rewrite both in twenty-fourths: 9/24 versus 16/24 shows 3/8 < 2/3. Jayden's mistake is the most common one in this skill — comparing top numbers while the pieces are still different sizes.

questions.question: Ella and Noah each bring a 1 L bottle of water to soccer practice. Ella drinks 2/5 of hers and Noah drinks 3/8 of his. Who drinks more, and does that person drink more or less than half a litre?
options: Noah, because 3 is more than 2; he drinks more than 1/2 L
Ella, because 2/5 = 16/40 and 3/8 = 15/40; she drinks less than 1/2 L
Noah, because eighths are bigger pieces than fifths; he drinks more than 1/2 L
Ella, because 2/5 = 16/40 and 3/8 = 15/40; she drinks more than 1/2 L
questions.explain: Use 40 as the common denominator: 2/5 = 16/40 and 3/8 = 15/40, so Ella drinks more, and since half of 40 is 20, her 16/40 is still under 1/2 L. The trap is stopping after picking the winner — drinking the most does not mean drinking more than half.

questions.question: Three students in a Victoria class report the fraction of their quiz they got right: 3/4, 7/10 and 2/5. Which fraction is the median (the middle value when they are ordered)?
options: 3/4, because 3 is the middle number among the numerators 3, 7 and 2, so it sits in the middle
2/5, because 5 is the middle denominator of 4, 10 and 5, so 2/5 must be the middle fraction
7/10, because in twentieths they are 15/20, 14/20 and 8/20, and 14/20 sits in the middle
There is no median until you add the three fractions and divide by 3 to find the middle
questions.explain: To find a median you must order the values first, so rename them all in twentieths: 15/20, 14/20 and 8/20 order as 8/20, 14/20, 15/20, putting 7/10 in the middle. Two traps here — ordering by numerators or denominators alone, and mixing up median (the middle value) with mean (the adding-and-sharing one).

questions.question: For a Burnaby bake sale, Jasmin uses 5/6 of a bag of flour and Theo uses 7/9 of an identical bag. Who uses more flour, and what common denominator shows it?
options: Theo, because 7 is more than 5
Theo, because ninths are bigger parts than sixths
Neither — they use the same, because each one is one part away from a full bag
Jasmin, because in eighteenths 5/6 = 15/18 and 7/9 = 14/18
questions.explain: Eighteen works for both denominators: 5/6 = 15/18 and 7/9 = 14/18, so Jasmin uses more. Being ‘one part away from a whole’ does not make fractions equal, because Jasmin's missing part (1/6) is larger than Theo's missing part (1/9).
